analysis.one_liner: Charges ranchers, miners, and federal hydropower customers market rates for using public lands and resources.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended several long-standing discounts on public resources. Federal dam power would have been priced to repay construction debt on a faster schedule, ranchers grazing cattle on national forest and Bureau of Land Management land would have paid fair market value instead of the current below-cost fee, and companies mining gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals on federal land would have paid a royalty of at least 12.5% of gross income — under the law as written then, they paid nothing. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never went anywhere: no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently absorb the difference between what ranchers and miners pay for federal resources and what those resources are worth. Federal hydropower ratepayers in some regions would pay more up front but the debt on the dams would be retired sooner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers subsidizing below-cost public land use

how_it_helps.text: Requires a royalty of at least 12.5% of gross income on hardrock minerals produced from federal mining claims, which are currently mined royalty-free under the general mining laws [S2] [S3].

Directs the Agriculture and Interior Departments to set an annual grazing fee equal to fair market value on national forest and BLM lands in the 16 contiguous Western states, replacing the existing below-cost fee formula [S2] [S3].

Requires that revenues from federal hydroelectric power sales be collected through uniform annual payments of equal principal and interest, starting when each project begins delivering power, so project debt is repaid on a standard schedule rather than at rates that delay repayment [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Western livestock ranchers would pay sharply higher grazing fees; hardrock mining companies would pay a royalty they have never paid on federal land; customers of federal hydropower, such as electric utilities and their ratepayers in regions served by federal dams, would pay higher rates to speed debt repayment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Western ranchers, mining companies, hydropower customers

drawbacks.text: The bill caps year-to-year grazing fee changes at 33.3% to soften the transition, but ranchers operating on thin margins could still face significantly higher costs, which could push some small operators off the land [S3].

Requiring faster debt repayment on federal hydroelectric projects would raise electricity prices for utilities and households in regions served by federal dams, a cost that falls partly on ordinary ratepayers, not just large industrial users [S2] [S3].
A 12.5% gross-income royalty is high by industry standards and critics argued it could make some marginal mining operations uneconomic, though under prior law operators paid nothing at all [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have ended real subsidies — royalty-free hardrock mining and below-cost grazing on federal land — that cost taxpayers money, and its 33.3% annual cap on grazing fee changes showed an attempt to ease the transition. The main honest cost is that some western ranchers and mining operations, and some hydropower ratepayers, would pay more for resources they currently get at a discount. The tradeoff is straightforward: public resources sold at a discount to private users versus public resources priced at what they are worth. The bill was never tested in debate, so questions about how the fee formula would work in practice were never examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there for the rest of the Congress, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on April 7, 1993 [S5].
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies, western ranchers, and federal hydropower customers kept the below-market rates the bill would have ended, and taxpayers kept paying the difference.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies, ranchers, and hydropower customers

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise grazing fees, impose a hardrock mining royalty, and speed federal hydropower debt repayment [S5].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 7, 1993 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress [S1] [S5].

against.name: Hardrock mining industry and western livestock ranchers
against.role: Industries that pay below-market rates for federal land and minerals
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising grazing fees and imposing mining royalties during the broader 1993-94 public lands fee debate; no specific lobbying on this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of any party, and never received a vote, so no partisan lineup was ever recorded [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 12.5% gross-income royalty on minerals mined from federal land, which operators currently extract without paying any royalty [S2] [S3]. The public's gain is the industry's cost. Under prior law, taxpayers received nothing for gold and silver taken from federal land.

The bill would have replaced the below-cost grazing fee with a fair market value fee on Forest Service and BLM lands in 16 western states [S2] [S3]. Ranchers currently graze livestock on public land at rates well below what private pasture costs.

industries.industry: Federal hydropower customers (utilities and their ratepayers)
industries.note: Utilities and households served by federal dams would have paid higher power rates, but those rates would have repaid the dams' construction debt on schedule instead of spreading it out at rates that delay repayment [S2] [S3]. The current discount is effectively subsidized by taxpayers.
